title: Buddham saranam gacchami
hookLine: a storm shelter, a friend's kitchen, a song in the car: where do you go?
tomorrow: why say the refuges three times? isn't once enough?

lines: A SHELTER, A KITCHEN, A SONG.
cards: A storm shelter is a refuge. So is the friend's kitchen you head to after a terrible day, or the song you put on in the car when the week is too loud. Nobody waits for a tornado to have one of those.
You go there on ordinary days too, and that's partly why it works when things go wrong. So yesterday's question has an answer already: refuge isn't only for danger.
In Pali, the line goes Buddham saranam gacchami, and the last word is the surprise.

teach.b: Word by word. Buddham: the Buddha, as the place you're headed. Saranam: refuge, shelter.
Gacchami: I go. Not I believe, not I agree.

teach.h: I GO: A VERB OF THE FEET.
teach.b: I go: a verb of the feet. The chant then goes to the dhamma, his teaching, and the sangha, the community who practice it. Three refuges.

The Dhammapada says that people driven by fear run to mountains, forests and sacred trees, and that this is not a safe refuge; the one who goes to the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha comes to see the way out of suffering.
So the danger it has in mind isn't a storm. It's the ordinary ache of a life that grasps. Here's a neighbor who says refuge out loud too.

teach.h: I SEEK REFUGE IN THE LORD OF MANKIND.
teach.b: The Qur'an closes with a short surah that opens, in Pickthall's English, "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind."

Shared ground: both put refuge into words you say, a turning-toward spoken by heart, and that line names its Lord as Lord of all people at once, mankind. One honest difference: there, refuge is sought in God.
Here, it's a teacher who woke up, his teaching and a community, and in his last days, the suttas say, the Buddha told his followers to be a refuge to themselves, with the dhamma as their refuge.
Different shelters, the same human need to go somewhere. I go for refuge.

how: In Theravada temples, after the homage, monks and lay people chant the three refuges in Pali: Buddham saranam gacchami, dhammam saranam gacchami, sangham saranam gacchami.

o: a vow to never leave home again
refuge, a shelter you go to
a word for a temple's front gate

games.q: the first refuge, word by word — tap the pairs.
p: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind

s: it means I go. going for refuge is a movement, not only an opinion.
the Dhammapada says mountains and sacred trees aren't a safe refuge
people driven by fear run there, it says; the three refuges are the way out of suffering.
going for refuge is only for emergencies
it's said on ordinary days, and the suffering it has in mind is the everyday ache of grasping.

games.q: a friend says going for refuge sounds like hiding from life. what's the fairest answer from today's lesson?
o: it's a going-toward: a teacher, a teaching and a community, on good days too.
they're right: it's for hiding until trouble passes, and then you stop.
it means the Buddha steps in and personally fixes things for you.
games.why: gacchami means I go. the refuge is the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha, and in the suttas he tells his followers to be a refuge to themselves, with the dhamma as their refuge.

practice: Count three places you already go when the week gets heavy, one on each finger: a person, a practice, a place. Thank each one quietly as you count it.
Then, if you'd like, say the line once, Buddham saranam gacchami, and rest with the breath as a fourth shelter, the one you carry.

wordCard.voice: Saranam. Refuge, shelter: where you go, on bad days and good ones. Word eight of a little Pali.

orig.note: Buddham saranam gacchami in Devanagari letters: to the Buddha I go for refuge.

carryVoice: Your line, said with your feet: I go for refuge. One week of Pali behind you.
